question: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

Under Regulation (EU) 2026/467 of 24 February 2026, Ukraine is required to repay its EUR 90 billion loan within 30 days of Russia’s payment of war reparations. Article 20(2)(l) provides, in turn, that outstanding amounts will remain in place indefinitely in the event of non-payment of reparations. And Article 20(2)(j)(iv) provides for repayment in the event of fraud or corruption on the part of Ukraine. However, the Regulation does not specify a competent authority, and neither OLAF nor the EPPO nor the Court of Auditors have jurisdiction over Ukraine. 1.

Who will be liable for repaying the principal of the loan (EUR 90 billion), and how much, if Russia refuses to pay reparations – will this liability fall on the 24 participating states in proportion to their GNI as a share of the total GNI of the 24 participating states, and when would it become due?
Has the Commission carried out a financial impact assessment for the scenario of Russia not paying reparations, or delaying payment for years, and if so, when will it be made public?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) Russia – as the aggressor state – is under an obligation to make full reparation for the damage caused by its war of aggression against Ukraine. Council Decision (CFSP) 2022/3351 and Council Regulation (EU) 2022/3342 prohibit transactions related to the management of reserves as well as assets of the Central Bank of Russia, including transactions with any legal person, entity or body acting on behalf of, or at the direction of, the Central Bank of Russia. In its conclusions of 27 June, 17 October and 19 December 2024, the European Council has stated that, subject to EU law, Russia’s assets should remain immobilised until Russia ceases its war of aggression against Ukraine and compensates Ukraine for the damage caused by that war. In that context, the EU has made clear that Russia is responsible for compensating Ukraine for the damage it has caused. The EU has further made clear that Russia’s assets should remain immobilised until Russia, inter alia, compensates Ukraine for the damage caused by that war. Such compensation from Russia will be used by Ukraine to repay the Ukraine Support Loan. Finally, it is noted that the Ukraine Support Loan is a limited-recourse loan, where Ukraine is only due to repay the principal of the loan when Russia pays reparations. Until such time, the principal of the loan will not fall due for payment and – as such – no one will repay the principal of the loan. The Commission closely monitors the EU’s contingent liabilities and their budgetary implications.
